The study was a randomized controlled trial (RCT) that compared a lifestyle intervention to a control condition in a sample of 330 overweight and obese women with infertility.
The study was designed as a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel-group study.

1) weight-loss interventions in obese infertile females do not improve pregnancy rate; 2) weight loss does not affect the quality of the oocytes retrieved during ovarian stimulation; and 3) weight loss does affect the quality of embryos obtained after in vitro fertilization.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of the immune system in the pathophysiology of obesity and its comorbidities.
the relationship between weight and fertility, and how this relationship is affected by weight loss.
the development of novel and effective strategies to treat obesity.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the study did not prove that weight loss improves birth rates in obese women.
there is no difference in the birth rate of obese infertile patients undergoing weight loss intervention compared with those undergoing standard fertility treatment.
there is no difference in the pregnancy rates of obese infertile patients undergoing IVF/ICSI with or without weight loss.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have shown that weight loss does not improve the live birth rate for women with obesity and infertility.
weight loss does not improve the chances of having a child for obese infertile couples.
the weight loss intervention does not seem to be beneficial for women who are obese and who have infertility.
The main takeaway from our work is that
weight loss is not a requirement for fertility treatment, says lead author Dr Elizabeth Ginsburg, of Brigham and Women’s Hospital and Harvard Medical School in Boston, Massachusetts, US.
